processing: Typical of Fenghuang Dancong: sun-withered, shaken and rested to partial oxidation, fired, rolled and dried or lightly roasted.
harvest_season: A mid-season bush; as with most Fenghuang Dancong, spring is the main picking.
appearance_dry: Typically long, dark brown strips, as with other Dancong.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear orange-yellow, as with other Dancong.
appearance_wet: Medium-sized leaves with a raised, bumpy surface, typically reddened at the edges.
taste_profile: A rich, lasting aroma and a full body, and it holds up over many steeps.

brewing.notes: Keep the first steeps quick, as with other Dancong. It is described as long-lasting, so keep going after you would normally stop.

vintage_note: Rarely listed and considered a scarce variety. As is usual for Dancong, it is sold by spring harvest of the current year, often with some months of rest after roasting.
description:
Ha Gu Lao is a Dancong cultivar native to Chao'an in Guangdong, nicknamed 'old toad'. The name comes from the leaf: a Chinese article on Dancong naming says its surface bulges like toad skin.

The plant is a small-arbor, medium-leaf, mid-season type. Dancong often take their names from an aroma, but this one is named for how the leaf looks, like several others in Fenghuang.

The tea is described as having a strong, lasting aroma, a full texture and good staying power across steeps. Little more is recorded about its specific flavour. Use the usual Dancong approach: gaiwan, hot water and quick pours.

It is listed among the rarer Dancong varieties, and spellings vary widely (Hagulao, Gegulao, 蛤蛄捞). Search for all of them when shopping, and ask the seller where the leaf comes from.
history: Little is documented about when the variety was selected or by whom. Modern tea references record it as a named cultivar from Chao'an county, and its name is explained by the leaf's toad-like surface.
